messages.subject: Estimating Model fit indices in polytomous model.
messages.subject_clean: Estimating Model fit indices in polytomous model.
messages.body_plain:
Dear Phil,

I have been thinking that "mirt" is a very precious package. It's seems like superman. ;)

However,
I want to estimate model fit indices like CFI, TLI, and RMESA in polytomous model.
How can I do it in version 1.2.1?

When I use version 0.9.x, I can calculate them in polytomous model.
But after updating, I can't calculate them in polytomous model.

I have to calculate them for doing my research.
Please give me some advice.

--
Best wishes,
Seongho Bae.

Master of Psychology in Industrial & Organizational Psychology (2014 ~ )

messages.subject: Re: Estimating Model fit indices in polytomous model.
messages.subject_clean: Estimating Model fit indices in polytomous model.
messages.body_plain:
Hi Seongho,

These indexes are still supported when using the M2() function, though it currently only supports dichotomous item types. After running a short simulation I noticed that fitIndicies() was not returning consistent Type I error results, so I removed it from the package and put a much better version of the M2 statistic in its own function. It now returns appropriate Type I error results for single and multiple-group models.

I will be supporting the M2* for polytomous items sometime (which is a further collapsed version of the M2 for even better stability) if/when I get the time to write it; unfortunately, the math is a bit laborious to work through, so it's implementation is not straightforward. Cheers.

Phil

I see, the mirt.model() definitions only work with numeric inputs (for now at least), so you'd need something more like

cmodel<-mirt.model('
F1 = 1-10
F2 = 11-20')

Where the numbers indicate which column in the data input should have a non-zero loading for the factor. Hope that helps.

Phil

On Thu, Apr 10, 2014 at 12:17 PM, Danilo Assis Pereira <dani...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Dear Dr. Phil,
>
> Finally, I run my model, but I saw that it is necessary to use 'mixmodel' when dealing with dichotomous and polythomous data...
> Actually, I have 3 questions:
>
> 1) How to run a mixed mirt in this model?
> cmodel<-mirt.model('
> F1 = 11,5,7,12
> F2 = 10,9,1,2
> F3 = 8,6,4,3')
> cmod<-mirt(data,cmodel) #mixedmirt, not mirt
> coef(cmod)
> #Dichotomous items are 3,4,6, and 8 (data mirt.txt)

Run the model with mirt(), mixedmirt() is something very different and will only makes sense if you've analysed IRT data in a mixed effects modelling framework (like models estimated with lme4::glmer()). The functions by default treat the itemtypes as '2PL' models if dichotomous, and 'graded' if polytomous, though these can be overwritten by using the itemtype=... argument.

>
> 2) Is it correct to transform total d (summed) into b (difficulty) calculating b=(-d/number of factors)?

I think this question is referring to the classical IRT parametrization, in which case no this is no the same. coef(..., IRTpars = TRUE) does the conversions for you, but not for multidimensional models.

>
> 3) How to cite mirt(1.2.1) package in my paper?

In R, type citation('mirt'). Cheers.

Phil

Phil

messages.subject: Re: data simulation with mirt
messages.subject_clean: data simulation with mirt
messages.body_plain:
If you prefer not to set up one large 'd' matrix of item intercepts directly, try constructing them separately given your latent Theta parameters. Try something like this:

```
library(mvtnorm)
Theta <- rmvnorm(1000, sigma = matrix(c(1, .5, .5, 1), 2)) #correlation of .5

#simulated dichotomous items first, slopes at 1, with simple structure
d <- matrix(rnorm(80))
a <- matrix(c(rep(1, 40), rep(0,80), rep(1,40)), 80)
dichitems <- simdata(a, d, 1000, Theta=Theta, itemtype = 'dich')

#now graded items, with 5 categories each
a2 <- matrix(c(rep(1, 20), rep(0,40), rep(1,20)), 40)
d2 <- matrix(rnorm(40*4), 40)
d2 <- t(apply(d2, 1, sort, decreasing=TRUE)) #sort since intercepts are ordered
polytomous <- simdata(a2, d2, 1000, Theta=Theta, itemtype = 'graded')

dat <- data.frame(dich=dichitems, poly=polytomous)

#estimate it
model <- mirt.model('F1 = 1-40, 81-100
                    F2 = 41-80, 101-120
                    COV = F1*F2')
mod <- mirt(dat, model)
summary(mod)
coef(mod)
```

Phil

Hi Jon,

Yes. If you passed the option SE=TRUE to obtain standard errors, the information matrix will be inside the estimated object. Just invert this to get the ACOV parameter matrix (parameters are also named and numbered here too for convenience).

dat <- expand.table(LSAT7)
mod <- mirt(dat, 1, SE=TRUE)
acov <- solve(mod@information)

Phil

messages.subject: Re: covariance matrix of item parameter estimates
messages.subject_clean: covariance matrix of item parameter estimates
messages.body_plain:
They are actually one and the same though looking at different pieces in the model, but you are correct that the @information slot doesn't involve theta; it has been integrated out of the equation, which is the marginal maximum-likelihood paradigm that the package uses. Information in both cases tells us basically how much 'information' either the data (in estimating the parameters) or the model (in predicting theta) contributes to estimating our parameters: the more information we have, the smaller the standard error. This relates directly to the curvature of the log-likelihood function, though I'll leave that for you too look into a bit more.

I don't know of any resources that are non-technical to talk about this topic, but if you haven't looked into what the observed and expected (i.e., Fisher) information matrices are in maximum-likelihood theory then I would highly recommend it since it is key to understanding a lot of ML theory. Here's a pdf that I found a while back which explained the topic relatively well, and touches on how the Sandwich covariance matrix works as well. Cheers.

Phil

My operating system was Ubuntu 14.04, R 3.1.0, RStudio, Openblas, and Intel i7 4770K processor.

Thanks.

--
Blessings,
Seongho.

The M2 function is far from optimized, though I plan to make it faster once I add polytomous item support. For now the implementation is written in pure R code with lots of loops and no parallel architecture support, so it's bound to be slow at times.

Phil

messages.subject_clean: mirt 1.3 on CRAN
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

mirt versions 1.3 is now on CRAN. In addition to adding a few new features and modifying some global parameters it also serves as a bugfix update for two dependent changes: R 3.1.0, and an update to the mvtnorm package (which is no longer imported due to this change). As usual, the change-log is available in the NEWS and NEWS.md file (https://github.com/philchalmers/mirt/blob/master/NEWS.md). Cheers.

Phil
